title: As a data engineer, I pick from a broad catalog of maintained connectors for the SaaS APIs, databases, and files my company actually uses
As a data engineer, I build a custom connector for a long-tail API with a supported framework or low-code builder, not a fork
As a data engineer, the catalog tells me each connector's maturity, support level, and maintainer before I depend on it
As a data engineer, syncs move only new and changed records — cursor and state management handled for me, not full reloads
As a data engineer, I replicate databases with log-based CDC (binlog/WAL) so I capture updates and deletes without hammering the source
As a data engineer, I can backfill history or resync a single table without rebuilding the whole pipeline
As a data engineer, I control sync frequency per pipeline — from sub-hour schedules to cron expressions and manual triggers
As a data engineer, upstream schema changes are detected and propagated by a policy I choose, instead of silently breaking loads
As an analytics engineer, loaded data lands as typed, deduplicated destination tables ready to query, not raw JSON blobs
As a data engineer, I define dependencies between pipeline steps and datasets, and the platform orchestrates runs in the right order
As a data engineer, I see end-to-end lineage of my datasets — which sources, steps, and transformations produced each table
As a data engineer, I run and test a pipeline locally against a lightweight destination before it touches production
As a data engineer, I see run status, logs, and row counts per sync, and failures alert me in Slack, email, or a webhook
As an analytics engineer, I can tell how fresh each destination table is and get warned when a pipeline misses its expected cadence
As a data engineer, transient failures retry automatically and interrupted syncs resume from checkpoints instead of restarting
As an analytics engineer, dbt transformations run against freshly loaded data as part of the pipeline, not on a blind timer
As a data engineer, my pipelines are plain code and config in my own repository — versioned, reviewed, and portable like any software
As a data engineer, I load to the major warehouses and lakes — Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, object storage — without changing pipelines
As an analytics engineer, I sync modeled warehouse data back into SaaS tools (CRM, ads, support) to activate it where teams work
As a data platform lead, the pricing model is published and predictable — I can estimate what a new source costs before connecting it
As an AI-native user, AI drafts a working connector from API documentation — auth, pagination, streams — that I review and ship
As an AI-native user, a coding agent can scaffold, configure, and run a complete pipeline headlessly through the CLI or API
As an AI-native user, an agent can check sync status, diagnose a failed run, and re-trigger it through an API or MCP server
As an AI-native user, pipelines load into vector stores and LLM-ready formats so my agents can retrieve what was synced
